title: How Vaccines Train the Body
summary: How the immune system fights germs, how vaccines safely teach it to recognize them, and why protecting many people helps keep everyone safer.
poll: Getting a vaccine helps other people, not just the person who gets it.

versions.title: Vaccines Help Us
versions.text:
Germs are so small. You can not see them. Some germs can make you sick. That is no fun.

Your body can fight germs. It has a team for that. The team is the immune system. It makes antibodies. They stick to germs. Then the germs can not hurt you.

A germ gets in for the first time. The team is slow. You may get sick. But the team will not lose track of it. The next time, it is fast. It wins!

A vaccine is like a drill. It shows the body a weak germ. Or it shows a bit of one. This can not make you sick. But the body learns how the germ looks. It makes antibodies. Now it is ready.

A shot may make your arm sore. That is OK. It will go away.

Some kids and grown-ups can not get a shot. But lots of us can get one. Then the germ can not spread well. That helps protect them, too. We all win.

versions.title: How Vaccines Help Us
versions.text:
Germs are tiny living things. They are too small to see. Some germs can make people sick.

Your body can fight germs. It is called the immune system. It is like a team of guards. The guards move in your blood. A bad germ gets in. Then they make antibodies. These grab the germ. Then it can not do harm.

The first time a germ gets in, the guards are slow. They do not know it yet. You may feel sick for a while. But the guards will know the germ. If it comes back, they fight it fast.

A vaccine helps the body learn early. It has a weak germ or a dead one. Some just have a small piece of a germ. It can not make you really sick. But the body still learns how the germ looks. It makes antibodies. Then it is ready for the real germ.

Your arm may be sore after a shot. It lasts a day or so. That is fine.

Lots of people get a vaccine. Then a germ has a hard time spreading. This helps protect babies and people who are sick.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Germs are tiny living things. They are much too small to see with your eyes. Most germs do no harm, but some can make people sick.

Luckily, your body can fight back. It has the immune system. This works like a team of guards. The guards move all through your blood. When a bad germ gets in, they make antibodies. Antibodies grab on to the germ. Then it can not do harm.

The first time a new germ gets in, the guards need time to learn about it. While they learn, you may feel sick. But the guards keep a memory of that germ. If it ever comes back, they know it at once and fight it fast.

A vaccine helps the body learn early, before it meets the real germ. A vaccine has a weak germ or a dead germ. Some have just a piece of one. It can not give you the real sickness. But the body still learns to spot the germ. It makes antibodies. Now it is ready.

After a shot, your arm may feel sore. You may feel tired for a day. These are normal signs that show the body is learning.

When many people get a vaccine, a germ has trouble spreading. That helps protect babies. It also helps people who are too sick to get the vaccine.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Germs are tiny living things. They are much too small to see without a microscope. Most germs do no harm, and some even help us. But a few kinds can make people sick.

Luckily, your body has its own defense team. It is called the immune system. It works like an army of guards that travel through your blood. When a harmful germ gets in, the guards make antibodies. Antibodies are special parts that lock on to the germ. Then it cannot do damage.

The first time a new germ gets in, the immune system needs a few days to learn how to fight it. During that time, you may feel sick. But the system keeps a memory of the germ. If the same germ comes back, the guards know it right away and stop it fast.

A vaccine lets the body practice before it meets the real germ. A vaccine holds a weak germ or a dead germ. Some hold just a harmless piece of one. It cannot give you the real illness. Even so, the immune system learns to spot the germ and makes antibodies. Now the body is ready.

After a vaccine, your arm may feel sore. You may feel tired for a day or two. These are normal signs that the body is learning.

When most people in a town get a vaccine, a germ has trouble spreading from person to person. That helps protect babies. It also helps people who are too sick to get the vaccine.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Every day, you meet millions of germs. They live on your hands, in the air, and on the things you touch. Most are harmless, and some even help you. But a few kinds of bacteria and viruses can cause an infection that makes people sick.

Luckily, your body has a strong defense team called the immune system. Special white blood cells travel through your body, looking for invaders. When they find a harmful germ, some of these cells make antibodies. Antibodies are made to lock on to one kind of germ. They mark it so other cells can destroy it.

The first time the immune system meets a new germ, it needs a few days to make the right antibodies. During that time, the germ can multiply, and you may feel sick. But after that, the body keeps memory cells that remember the germ. If the same germ comes back, the body knows it quickly and often stops it before you feel ill.

A vaccine lets the body practice without the danger of the real disease. Some vaccines contain a weakened or killed germ. Others hold only a harmless piece of it. None of these can cause the full illness. Still, the immune system learns to spot the germ, makes antibodies, and keeps memory cells.

After a vaccine, some people have a sore arm or feel tired for a day or two. These are usually signs that the body is building protection.

Vaccines also protect the whole community. When most people are immune, a germ has trouble spreading. This helps protect new babies. It also protects people with some illnesses who cannot get certain vaccines.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Every day, you encounter millions of microscopic germs. They live on your hands, float in the air, and cover the objects you touch. Most are harmless, and some are actually beneficial. However, certain bacteria and viruses can cause an infection that makes people seriously ill.

Fortunately, your body has a powerful defense force called the immune system. Specialized white blood cells patrol your body, searching for invaders. When they detect a harmful germ, some of these cells produce antibodies. Antibodies are proteins precisely shaped to attach to one particular germ, marking it so that other cells can destroy it.

The first time the immune system encounters an unfamiliar germ, it requires several days to produce the correct antibodies. During that period, the germ can multiply, and you may feel ill. Afterward, however, the immune system retains memory cells that remember the germ. If the same germ returns, the body recognizes it rapidly and often defeats it before any symptoms appear.

A vaccine allows the body to rehearse its response without facing the danger of the actual disease. Some vaccines contain a weakened or inactivated germ. Others contain only a harmless fragment of it. None of these can cause the full illness. Nevertheless, the immune system learns to recognize the germ, produces antibodies, and stores memory cells for the future.

In the 1790s, an English doctor named Edward Jenner showed that material from a mild cattle disease called cowpox could protect people from a deadly disease called smallpox. His work led to the first vaccine.

After a vaccination, some people experience a sore arm or mild tiredness for a day or two. These temporary effects usually indicate that the body is building protection.

Vaccines also protect the entire community. When most people are immune, a germ has difficulty spreading from person to person. This shields newborn babies and people with certain medical conditions who cannot receive particular vaccines.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Every day, you encounter millions of microscopic germs. They inhabit your hands, drift through the air, and cover nearly every object you touch. Most are harmless. Many are even helpful. However, certain bacteria and viruses, which scientists call pathogens, can cause infections that make people seriously ill.

Fortunately, your body possesses a sophisticated defense network called the immune system. Specialized white blood cells patrol your bloodstream and tissues, searching for invaders. When they detect a harmful pathogen, some of these cells manufacture antibodies. These proteins are precisely shaped to attach to one particular germ and mark it so that other cells can destroy it.

The first time the immune system encounters an unfamiliar pathogen, it requires several days to produce the appropriate antibodies, and during that period the germ can multiply and make you ill. Afterward, however, the immune system retains memory cells that remember the invader. If the same pathogen returns, the body recognizes it rapidly and frequently defeats it before any symptoms appear. This lasting protection is called immunity.

A vaccine allows the body to develop immunity without confronting the danger of the actual disease. Some vaccines contain a weakened or inactivated pathogen, while others contain only a harmless fragment of it, or instructions that help the body's own cells make that fragment. None of these can cause the full illness. Nevertheless, the immune system learns to recognize the germ, produces antibodies, and stores memory cells. Some vaccines require more than one dose to build strong protection.

In the 1790s, an English physician named Edward Jenner demonstrated that material from cowpox, a mild cattle disease, could protect people from smallpox, a deadly illness. Nearly two centuries later, after a worldwide vaccination effort, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

After a vaccination, some people experience a sore arm or mild tiredness for a day or two. These temporary effects usually indicate that the body is building protection.

Vaccines also protect the entire community. When most people are immune, a pathogen has difficulty spreading from person to person. This shields vulnerable people, such as newborn babies and people with certain medical conditions who cannot receive particular vaccines.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Every day, you encounter millions of microscopic germs. They inhabit your hands, drift through the atmosphere, and coat nearly every object you touch. Most are harmless. Many are genuinely beneficial. However, certain bacteria and viruses, which scientists classify as pathogens, can cause infections that make people seriously ill.

Fortunately, your body possesses a sophisticated defense network called the immune system. Specialized white blood cells continuously patrol your bloodstream and tissues, searching for invaders. When they detect a harmful pathogen, some of these cells manufacture antibodies, which are proteins precisely shaped to attach to one particular germ and identify it for destruction by other cells.

The first time the immune system encounters an unfamiliar pathogen, it requires several days to generate the appropriate antibodies, and during that interval the germ can multiply. Afterward, however, the immune system retains memory cells that remember the invader. If the same pathogen returns, the body recognizes it rapidly and frequently defeats it before any symptoms develop. This lasting protection is called immunity.

A vaccine allows the body to develop immunity without confronting the danger of the actual disease. Certain vaccines contain a weakened or inactivated pathogen, while others contain only a harmless fragment of it, or genetic instructions that enable the body's own cells to manufacture that fragment temporarily. None of these can cause the full illness. Nevertheless, the immune system learns to recognize the germ, produces antibodies, and stores memory cells. Some vaccines require more than one dose to establish durable protection.

In the 1790s, an English physician named Edward Jenner demonstrated that material from cowpox, a relatively mild cattle disease, could protect people from smallpox, a devastating illness. Nearly two centuries later, after a coordinated international vaccination campaign, smallpox was officially declared eradicated in 1980.

After receiving a vaccine, some people have a sore arm. Others feel mild fatigue for a day or two. These temporary effects generally indicate that the immune system is actively building protection.

Vaccines also safeguard the entire community. When most people are immune, a pathogen has difficulty spreading from person to person. This shields vulnerable individuals, including newborn babies and people with particular medical conditions who cannot safely receive certain vaccines.

versions.title: How Vaccines Train the Body
versions.text:
Every day, you encounter millions of microscopic germs, which inhabit your hands, drift through the atmosphere, and coat nearly every object you touch. The overwhelming majority are harmless, and many are genuinely beneficial; however, certain bacteria and viruses, which scientists classify as pathogens, can cause infections that make people seriously ill.

Fortunately, your body possesses a sophisticated defense network called the immune system. Specialized white blood cells continuously patrol your bloodstream and tissues, searching for invaders, and when they detect a harmful pathogen, some of these cells manufacture antibodies, which are proteins precisely configured to attach to one particular microorganism and identify it for destruction by other cells.

The first time the immune system encounters an unfamiliar pathogen, it requires several days to generate the appropriate antibodies, and during that interval the microorganism can multiply and make you ill. Subsequently, however, the immune system retains memory cells that remember the invader, so if the identical pathogen returns, the body recognizes it rapidly and frequently defeats it before any symptoms develop. This lasting protection is called immunity.

A vaccine enables the body to develop immunity without confronting the danger of the actual disease. Certain vaccines contain a weakened or inactivated pathogen, while others contain only a harmless fragment of it, or genetic instructions that enable the body's own cells to manufacture that fragment temporarily. None of these can cause the full illness. Even so, the immune system learns to recognize the microorganism, produces antibodies, and stores memory cells. Some vaccines require more than one dose to establish durable protection, and scientists evaluate every vaccine through extensive testing before it is approved for widespread use.

In the 1790s, an English physician named Edward Jenner demonstrated that material from cowpox, a relatively mild cattle disease, could protect people from smallpox, a devastating illness that had killed enormous numbers of people throughout history. Nearly two centuries later, following a coordinated international vaccination campaign, smallpox was officially declared eradicated in 1980, an accomplishment that remains one of the greatest achievements in the history of medicine.

After receiving a vaccine, some people have a sore arm. Others feel mild fatigue for a day or two. These temporary effects generally indicate that the immune system is actively constructing protection.

Vaccines also safeguard the entire community. When most people are immune, a pathogen has considerable difficulty spreading from person to person, which shields vulnerable individuals, including newborn babies and people with particular medical conditions who cannot safely receive certain vaccines.

keyWords.definition: a tiny living thing that can make you sick
keyWords.example: We wash our hands with soap to get rid of germs.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the parts of the body that fight sickness; the immune system is the body's team against germs
keyWords.example: Sleep and good food help keep your immune system strong.

keyWords.definition: a tiny part the body makes to grab and stop one kind of germ
keyWords.example: The doctor said my blood had antibodies against that sickness.

keyWords.definition: a medicine that teaches the body to fight a germ before it meets the real germ
keyWords.example: The nurse gave my little brother his vaccine at the clinic.

keyWords.definition: to keep someone or something safe from harm
keyWords.example: A helmet protects your head when you ride a bike.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How doctors fix broken bones
Why all germs are good for you
How vaccines help the body fight germs
Where to buy medicine for a cold
questions.why: The article explains how the body fights germs and how vaccines help it get ready.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about broken bones.
wrong.B: The article says some germs can make people sick.
wrong.D: The article does not tell where to buy medicine.

questions.stem: What does the immune system do?
options: It fights germs that get into the body.
It helps the body grow taller each year.
It moves food from the mouth to the belly.
It keeps the body warm in the winter.
questions.why: The article says the immune system is the body's team that fights germs.

wrong.B: The article does not connect the immune system to growing taller.
wrong.C: Moving food is not the job described in the article.
wrong.D: The article does not say the immune system keeps you warm.

questions.stem: What is inside a vaccine?
options: Strong germs that make you very sick
Sugar and water to give you energy
Tiny guards from another person
A weak germ or a small piece of a germ
questions.why: The article says a vaccine has a weak germ, a dead germ, or just a piece of a germ.

wrong.A: The article says a vaccine cannot give you the real sickness.
wrong.B: The article does not say vaccines are made of sugar and water.
wrong.C: The body makes its own guards; the vaccine does not bring them.

questions.stem: In the article, what are antibodies?
options: Germs that make people sick
Things the body makes to grab germs
Shots that doctors give to kids
Cells that carry food in the blood
questions.why: The article says the immune system makes antibodies, and they stick to or grab germs.

wrong.A: Antibodies fight germs; they are not germs.
wrong.C: A shot is how a vaccine is given, not an antibody.
wrong.D: The article does not say antibodies carry food.

questions.stem: What happens when the same germ gets into the body a second time?
options: The body forgets it and gets very sick.
The body knows it and fights it fast.
The germ turns into a vaccine.
The body makes no antibodies at all.
questions.why: The article says the body remembers a germ, so the next time it fights it fast.

wrong.A: The article says the body does not forget the germ.
wrong.C: Germs do not turn into vaccines.
wrong.D: The body makes antibodies to fight the germ.

questions.stem: Why is a vaccine like practice for the body?
options: It makes the body run and exercise.
It gives the body the real sickness.
It teaches the body to stop eating.
It lets the body learn a germ safely.
questions.why: A vaccine shows the body a weak germ or a piece of one, so the body learns it without getting really sick, just like practicing before a real game.

wrong.A: The practice is learning about a germ, not exercise.
wrong.B: The article says a vaccine cannot give you the real sickness.
wrong.C: Vaccines have nothing to do with eating.

questions.stem: Some people cannot get a vaccine. How can other people help keep them safe?
options: By getting vaccines so germs spread less
By giving them lots of sweet food
By keeping all the windows open
By staying away from all doctors
questions.why: The article says that when many people get a vaccine, a germ cannot spread well, and that protects people who cannot get one.

wrong.B: The article does not say sweet food stops germs.
wrong.C: The article does not talk about windows.
wrong.D: Staying away from doctors would not stop germs from spreading.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell readers that a sore arm is normal?
options: To warn readers never to get a shot
To explain how germs get into the body
To show it is not a reason to worry
To tell who found the immune system
questions.why: The author says a sore arm is normal and goes away, so readers know it is nothing to be afraid of.

wrong.A: The author explains that vaccines help, not that people should avoid them.
wrong.B: That part is about the shot, not about how germs get in.
wrong.D: The article does not say who found the immune system.

LOW.prompt: Explain how a vaccine helps your body get ready to fight a germ. Use at least two facts from the article.

keyWords.definition: a sickness caused by germs getting into the body
keyWords.example: The doctor cleaned the cut so it would not get an infection.

keyWords.definition: something that enters a place where it does not belong
keyWords.example: The ants treated the beetle as an invader and chased it away.
Weeds can multiply fast if no one pulls them out.
The weakened storm brought only a little rain.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who live in the same area
keyWords.example: Our community planted trees along the main road.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Vaccines safely teach the immune system to fight germs.
All germs are dangerous and must be avoided at all times.
White blood cells are the only cells found in the body.
Vaccines work by giving people the full illness first.
questions.why: The article explains how the immune system fights germs and how vaccines let it practice without the real disease.

wrong.B: The article says most germs are harmless and some are helpful.
wrong.C: The article describes white blood cells but never says they are the only cells.
wrong.D: The article says vaccines cannot cause the full illness.

questions.stem: According to the article, what do antibodies do?
options: They carry oxygen from the lungs to the heart.
They give the body energy when it is tired.
They lock on to a germ and mark it to be destroyed.
They turn harmful germs into helpful germs.
questions.why: The article says antibodies lock on to one kind of germ and mark it so other cells can destroy it.

wrong.A: The article does not say antibodies carry oxygen.
wrong.B: Antibodies fight germs; they do not give energy.
wrong.D: Antibodies mark germs for destruction; they do not change them into helpful ones.

questions.stem: What does the article say some vaccines contain?
options: A strong germ that causes the full disease
A weakened or killed germ
White blood cells taken from an animal
Medicine that kills every germ in the body
questions.why: The article states that some vaccines contain a weakened or killed germ, and others hold only a harmless piece.

wrong.A: The article says vaccines cannot cause the full illness.
wrong.C: The body makes its own white blood cells; vaccines do not contain them.
wrong.D: The article does not say vaccines kill every germ.

questions.stem: In the phrase "the germ can multiply," what does multiply mean?
options: to do a math problem
to become weaker and smaller
to hide inside a cell
to increase in number
questions.why: While the immune system is still learning, the germs grow in number, which is why a person can feel sick.

wrong.A: Multiply can mean a math operation, but not when describing germs.
wrong.B: This is the opposite of what happens to the germs.
wrong.C: The sentence is about germs growing, not hiding.

questions.stem: Why can the body often stop a germ it has met before?
options: The germ is always weaker the second time.
White blood cells stop working after an illness.
Memory cells help the body recognize it quickly.
The body makes new germs to fight the old ones.
questions.why: The article says the immune system keeps memory cells, so it knows a returning germ quickly and can stop it.

wrong.A: The article does not say germs get weaker; the body gets better prepared.
wrong.B: White blood cells keep working; the article never says they stop.
wrong.D: The body makes antibodies, not new germs.

questions.stem: Why might a person feel tired for a day after getting a vaccine?
options: The immune system is busy building protection.
The vaccine has given them the full disease.
The vaccine has removed all their antibodies.
Their memory cells have forgotten every germ.
questions.why: The article says mild effects like tiredness are usually signs that the body is building protection.

wrong.B: The article says vaccines cannot cause the full illness.
wrong.C: A vaccine helps the body make antibodies; it does not remove them.
wrong.D: Vaccines help the body store memory cells, not forget germs.

questions.stem: If very few people in a town were vaccinated, what would most likely happen?
options: Germs would stop spreading on their own.
Newborn babies would be safer than before.
Memory cells would form without any germs.
A germ could spread more easily among people.
questions.why: The article says a germ has trouble spreading when most people are immune, so with few people protected it could spread more easily.

wrong.A: The article gives no reason to think germs would stop on their own.
wrong.B: Babies are protected when most people are immune, so they would be less safe.
wrong.C: Memory cells form after the body meets a germ or a vaccine.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By telling the events of one doctor's life in order
By explaining how the body fights germs, then how vaccines help
By comparing two different diseases from long ago
By listing the problems with modern medicines today
questions.why: The article first explains germs and the immune system, then shows how vaccines use that system, and ends with how vaccines protect the community.

wrong.A: The article is not a life story of one doctor.
wrong.C: The article does not mainly compare two diseases.
wrong.D: The article does not list problems with medicine.

MID.prompt: Explain why vaccines protect not only the person who gets one but also the whole community. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how vaccines protect one person.
I explained how they protect the community, using details from the article.
I connected my ideas with words like because and so.

keyWords.definition: a germ, such as a bacterium or virus, that can cause disease
keyWords.example: Boiling water kills many pathogens that could make people ill.

keyWords.definition: the body's lasting protection against a particular disease
keyWords.example: After her illness, she had immunity to that kind of fever.

keyWords.definition: a measured amount of a medicine taken at one time
keyWords.example: The pharmacist explained when to take the second dose.

keyWords.definition: to destroy something completely so that it no longer exists
keyWords.example: The city worked for years to eradicate the mosquitoes that spread disease.
Young seedlings are vulnerable to strong winds.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Smallpox was the only disease ever controlled by vaccines.
Vaccines train the immune system safely and protect communities.
The immune system cannot defend the body without medicine.
Pathogens are mostly harmful and are found only in hospitals.
questions.why: The article explains how vaccines let the immune system build immunity without the real disease and how they protect whole communities.

wrong.A: Smallpox is one example; the article does not say it is the only one.
wrong.C: The article describes how the immune system defends the body on its own.
wrong.D: The article says most germs are harmless and they are found everywhere.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is immunity?
options: A type of germ that lives in cattle
A medicine that kills all bacteria
The process of germs multiplying
Lasting protection against a pathogen

wrong.B: Immunity is protection inside the body, not a medicine.
wrong.C: Germs multiplying is what happens before the body is protected.

It became a mild disease of cattle.
It spread to more countries than before.
It was renamed cowpox by scientists.

wrong.B: Cowpox, not smallpox, is the mild cattle disease.
wrong.D: Cowpox and smallpox are two different diseases.

questions.stem: In the article, the word vulnerable describes people who are—
options: very strong and rarely ill
trained to give vaccines
easily harmed by disease
unable to catch any germ

wrong.A: This is the opposite of vulnerable.
wrong.B: The article does not use the word for health workers.
wrong.D: Vulnerable people can catch germs; that is why they need protection.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do some vaccines require more than one dose?
options: To build strong, lasting protection
Because the first dose causes the illness
To replace the body's white blood cells
Because memory cells form only in adults
questions.why: The article says some vaccines need more than one dose to build strong, durable protection.

wrong.B: The article says vaccines cannot cause the full illness.
wrong.C: Vaccines train white blood cells; they do not replace them.
wrong.D: The article does not say memory cells form only in adults.

questions.stem: Why might Edward Jenner's work with cowpox be seen as the start of vaccines?
options: It proved that germs did not really exist.
It showed that cattle can never become sick.
A mild illness gave protection from a deadly one.
He found white blood cells using a microscope.
questions.why: Jenner used material from mild cowpox to protect people from deadly smallpox, the same idea vaccines use today: a safe exposure that builds protection.

wrong.A: The article never says Jenner proved germs did not exist.
wrong.B: Cowpox is a disease of cattle, so cattle do get sick.
wrong.D: The article does not say Jenner discovered white blood cells.

questions.stem: Why can a vaccine that contains only a harmless fragment of a pathogen still protect someone?
options: The fragment slowly grows into a full pathogen.
The immune system learns to recognize the fragment.
The fragment destroys every germ in the body.
The fragment replaces the person's memory cells.
questions.why: The immune system learns the shape of the fragment, makes antibodies, and stores memory cells, so it can recognize the real pathogen later.

wrong.A: The article says these vaccines cannot cause the full illness.
wrong.C: The fragment trains the body; it does not destroy germs itself.
wrong.D: The body creates memory cells; the fragment does not replace them.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the history of Edward Jenner and smallpox?
options: To argue that cattle should be kept away from people
To explain how white blood cells patrol the body
To describe the side effects of modern vaccines
To show that vaccines have a long, successful history
questions.why: The paragraph moves from Jenner's first vaccine in the 1790s to the eradication of smallpox, showing how vaccines have succeeded over time.

wrong.A: The paragraph does not argue about keeping cattle away.
wrong.B: White blood cells are explained in an earlier paragraph.
wrong.C: Side effects are described in a different paragraph.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say that getting a vaccine is a way of helping others, not only yourself. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
